title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 17
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Monarch Butterfly Migration
passages.text:
The monarch butterfly's multi-generational migration across North America is one of nature's most remarkable long-distance movements. Each autumn, millions of monarchs from Canada and the northern United States travel southward to overwintering sites in the mountain forests of central Mexico, traversing distances exceeding 3,000 kilometres. No individual butterfly completes the entire round-trip; instead, the migration involves four distinct generations per year, with only the autumn generation—called the 'super-generation'—possessing the extended lifespan necessary to survive the winter and return northward in spring.

The physiological transformation enabling the super-generation's remarkable longevity involves complex hormonal changes. These generation monarchs exhibit developmental diapause, a suspension of reproductive maturity triggered by seasonal photoperiod changes and declining temperatures. Diapause triggers metabolic suppression, reducing energy expenditure and enabling individuals to live six to eight months rather than the typical two to six weeks of other generations. This extended lifespan allows sufficient energy reserves for the metabolically expensive journey to Mexico and survival through months of dormancy in mountain oyamel forests at elevations between 2,400 and 3,600 metres, where temperatures remain cool enough to minimize activity while avoiding lethal freezing.

The navigation mechanisms underlying this extraordinary journey have fascinated researchers for decades. Monarchs possess a sun compass—a biological timekeeping system that uses the sun's position combined with an internal circadian clock to determine direction. The brain structure responsible for this navigation, the central complex, contains specialized neurons expressing cryptochromes, light-sensitive proteins enabling precise directional orientation. Magnetic field detection also contributes to navigation, mediated by iron-containing proteins in the antennae. The integration of multiple sensory inputs—solar position, magnetic fields, celestial cues, and possibly olfactory landmarks—creates a sophisticated navigational system compensating for wind drift and environmental obstacles across vast distances.

Conservation concerns regarding monarch populations have intensified dramatically over two decades. Eastern populations (originating from Canada and eastern United States) have declined by approximately 80 percent since the 1990s, with overwintering colonies in Mexico shrinking from historical estimates of 1 billion individuals to current counts of 30–100 million. Western populations show greater stability but remain vulnerable. Three primary threats converge to drive population decline: habitat loss throughout the migration corridor, climate change disrupting phenological synchronization, and widespread herbicide application eliminating milkweed—the sole larval food plant. Deforestation in Mexican overwintering forests, particularly conversion to agriculture, has directly destroyed critical refuge areas while expanding development fragments remaining habitat.

International conservation efforts have expanded in recent years to address this biodiversity crisis. Mexico, Canada, and the United States established the Trilateral Commission for Wildlife Conservation in the 1990s to coordinate monarch protection across jurisdictional boundaries. Conservation initiatives focus on milkweed restoration throughout the migration corridor, particularly in the United States where agricultural intensification and pesticide use have eliminated native milkweed populations. Protected areas in Mexico now legally safeguard critical overwintering forests, though enforcement remains inconsistent. Citizen science programs, particularly the Monarch Watch and Journey North initiatives, engage thousands of volunteers in tagging and monitoring migrations, providing crucial data on population dynamics and movement patterns.

passages.title: The Great Barrier Reef: Ecology
passages.text:
The Great Barrier Reef, stretching approximately 2,300 kilometres along Australia's northeastern coast, is the world's largest coral reef system and a biodiversity hotspot of global significance. Comprising approximately 2,900 individual reefs and supporting over 1,500 fish species, 400 coral species, and countless other organisms, the reef generates roughly 60 billion dollars annually in ecosystem services including tourism, fisheries, and coastal protection. This extraordinary ecosystem emerged over multiple marine transgression cycles spanning millions of years, creating complex three-dimensional habitat structures supporting intricate ecological relationships unparalleled in most terrestrial environments.

Coral biology underpins reef ecosystems through symbiotic relationships fundamentally different from most animals. Reef-building corals are animal hosts harbouring zooxanthellae—photosynthetic dinoflagellate algae living within coral tissues. This mutualistic partnership supplies corals with up to 90 percent of their energy requirements through photosynthetically produced sugars, enabling corals to build massive calcium carbonate skeletons supporting reef structure. Zooxanthellae receive protection and access to high-quality light in shallow reef waters. This co-evolution has produced tremendous ecological success, with coral reef ecosystems occupying less than 0.1 percent of ocean floor yet supporting roughly 25 percent of known marine fish species, demonstrating extraordinary biodiversity concentration.

Reef ecosystems maintain complex trophic structures supporting diverse feeding strategies. Herbivorous fish and sea urchins consume algae, preventing algal overgrowth that would smother corals and degrade reef structure. Corallivorous fish feed directly on coral tissues, while massive assemblages of planktivorous fish harvest zooplankton drifting across reef boundaries. Predatory sharks and groupers regulate herbivore and omnivore populations, preventing any single species from achieving dominance. Nocturnal invertebrates including crustaceans and molluscs emerge at night to exploit available resources, creating temporal partitioning that maximizes resource utilization. This ecological complexity produces remarkable stability, enabling reefs to recover from periodic disturbances through redundancy—multiple species occupying similar ecological roles—providing functional insurance against localized extinctions.

Climate change and ocean acidification pose unprecedented threats to reef ecosystems. Coral bleaching occurs when elevated sea temperatures trigger zooxanthellae expulsion, depriving corals of their primary energy source and ultimately causing mortality if prolonged beyond several weeks. The 1998 global bleaching event killed approximately 16 percent of reef-building corals worldwide; the 2016 event destroyed 30 percent of Great Barrier Reef corals. Ocean acidification—driven by seawater absorption of anthropogenic CO2—reduces carbonate ion concentration, making calcium carbonate precipitation energetically expensive and dissolving existing skeleton structures. Projections indicate that if atmospheric CO2 continues increasing, ocean pH may drop sufficiently to eliminate reef-building conditions entirely within this century.

Management and conservation strategies for reef ecosystems must address these multifaceted threats while sustaining human communities dependent on reef resources. Marine protected areas have expanded throughout the Great Barrier Reef, with no-take zones now covering approximately 33 percent of the system, reducing fishing pressure and facilitating population recovery. Restoration programs attempt to rehabilitate damaged reefs through coral transplantation and assisted evolution—selective breeding of heat-tolerant coral lines. However, these interventions remain insufficient without aggressive greenhouse gas emissions reductions limiting future warming and acidification. International collaboration through the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority coordinates management across jurisdictional scales, while scientific monitoring programs track ecosystem health indicators essential for adaptive management.

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes the multi-generational nature and super-generation adaptations (A), the sophisticated navigation system (C), and conservation threats (D).
options: A. Monarch migration is completed by multiple generations, with only the autumn super-generation surviving winter through extended lifespan and developmental diapause.
B. Monarchs use only solar navigation without any other sensory inputs.
C. Monarchs possess a sophisticated multi-sensory navigation system integrating solar, magnetic, and celestial cues.
D. Habitat loss, climate change, and milkweed elimination drive severe eastern population declines, with international conservation efforts attempting to restore populations.
E. Western monarch populations have increased significantly in recent decades.
F. Mexico's government has completely eliminated all threats to monarch overwintering habitat.
